_meta.method: Web search result summaries/abstract snippets only. Page fetching was blocked in this session (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov and www.jssm.org are outside the allowed network domains) and the shared web-search budget ran out, so table values come from snippets and were not checked against full texts. source_id 'CALC' = own simulation; 'memory' = unverified prior knowledge.
_meta.angle_conventions: Shoulder/hip 'alignment' or 'turn': 0 = line parallel to the net (chest facing net), 90 = side-on. Elbow/knee 'included angle': 180 = straight. 'flexion': 0 = straight. Racket face: degrees closed (tilted forward) from vertical. Launch/path angles: degrees above horizontal.
_meta.units_note: Besides the requested units, a few metrics use deg/s, m/s and %.
_meta.handedness: All left/right wording assumes a right-handed player.

metrics.definition: Shoulder-line angle to the baseline at the end of the initial unit turn (0 = facing net, 90 = side-on)
metrics.note: Yandell high-speed video description: 'unit turn gets the shoulders to about 45 degrees'. Qualitative video estimate, not mocap.

metrics.definition: Shoulder-line angle to the baseline at completion of the full turn (end of backswing)
metrics.note: Yandell: 'at least 90 degrees to the baseline, usually a little more'; full left-arm stretch across the body adds another 10-20 deg past perpendicular. Medvedev is ~90 because his left elbow stays bent.

metrics.definition: Maximum shoulder-vs-pelvis (hip) separation angle; negative = shoulders rotated further back than hips
metrics.note: ATP professionals n=6, 400 Hz Vicon. Range = cross-court (-28.7, SD 9.5) vs down-the-line (-25.4, SD 8.9). Column labels were inferred from the table row surfaced in a search snippet (third value equals the mean of the first two); not checked against full text.

metrics.definition: Same as above for high-performance (national-level, non-ATP) players
metrics.note: n=7. Cross-court -34.7 (SD 10.1), down-the-line -31.2 (SD 9.9). Group differences in peak angles were NOT significant - the paper says max racquet/shoulder/hip alignment angles were similar between levels; timing differed. Label inference as above.

metrics.definition: Relative increase of peak trunk axial rotation (before impact) when ball speed goes from slow to fast
metrics.note: Seeley 2011: several dominant-side peak joint angles prior to impact increased from slow to fast forehands: trunk rotation +28%, knee flexion +27%. Absolute degrees not captured.

metrics.definition: Relative increase of peak knee flexion before impact, slow -> fast forehand
metrics.note: Harder shots = deeper knee bend. Absolute values not captured.

metrics.definition: Front (left, for right-hander) knee included angle after the backswing (180 = straight leg)
metrics.note: Two groups of 6 players (group means 128.7 and 140.4). Rear/right knee about 113-114 in both groups. Small sample, source only seen as ResearchGate listing - treat as indicative.

metrics.definition: Rear (right, for right-hander) knee included angle after the backswing (180 = straight leg)
metrics.note: See above. i.e. roughly 65 deg of knee flexion on the loading leg.

metrics.definition: Optimum knee flexion in the preparatory (ready) stance for initiating quick trunk rotation
metrics.note: Yamamoto (1996) as cited in Nesbit et al. 2008. Flexion from straight (i.e. included angle about 155).

metrics.definition: Average loss of racket velocity when knee positioning and range of motion are reduced (stiff/straight legs) in a forward-dynamics model driven by real swings
metrics.note: 16 female college players, closed-stance forehand. Exaggerating knee motion also cost 17%. Rear-knee range of motion mattered more than its starting angle. Figures from a secondary copy of the abstract.

metrics.definition: Share of forehands hit from an open (incl. semi-open) stance in professional match play
metrics.note: 2,479 forehands by 20 professionals; no sex difference. Falls to 65.4% in favourable (time-rich) situations. Older, unsourced claim (Schonborn 1999): ~90%.

metrics.definition: Median ball-speed gain of square (neutral) stance over open stance
metrics.note: 42 players, 3,280 shots: +6 km/h in lateral running, +4 km/h in diagonal-inside running; accuracy and metabolic cost not significantly different. Player level not verified (population tag approximate).

metrics.definition: Shoulder-line angle to the net at contact (0 = parallel to net / chest facing net, 90 = side-on)
metrics.note: Yandell: spectrum from ~45 deg (more neutral-stance hitters) to parallel to the net (open-stance, straight-arm hitters). Forward shoulder rotation from full turn to finish is ~90 deg (neutral stance) up to ~180 deg (common in pro open-stance forehands).

metrics.definition: Pelvis axial angular velocity at impact
metrics.note: ATP pros 295 vs high-performance 168 deg/s. Unit extends the schema list.

metrics.definition: Upper-trunk axial angular velocity at impact
metrics.note: ATP pros 453 vs high-performance 292 deg/s. Levels differ in rotation speed/timing, not in peak angles.

metrics.definition: Horizontal linear speed of the hitting shoulder (peak)
metrics.note: Elite 3.0 +/- 0.4 vs high-performance 2.5 +/- 0.4 m/s (review citing Landlinger 2010a). The Sports Biomechanics abstract (S2) gives 2.0 vs 1.2 m/s at impact.

metrics.definition: Hitting-arm elbow included angle at impact, eastern-grip players (180 = straight)
metrics.note: Review citing Elliott et al. 1989/1997: eastern grip ~130 deg, more western grips ~100 deg. Elbow and wrist positions at impact are stable shot-to-shot (Knudson 1990).

metrics.definition: Hitting-arm elbow included angle at impact, western-grip players
metrics.note: See above.

metrics.definition: Frontal-plane carrying angle of the elbow measured on video frames with the elbow as close as possible to full extension just before impact
metrics.note: Top-25 ATP players. Not a flexion angle; included only as evidence that many top men approach full elbow extension before contact.

metrics.definition: Average groundstroke contact height above the court (all groundstrokes, Hawk-Eye, Australian Open)
metrics.note: About waist height. Secondary summary of Reid et al. Hawk-Eye work; extracted PDF text partly garbled. Roughly 0.51 x height for a 1.88 m player (height assumption from memory).

metrics.definition: Average groundstroke contact height above the court (all groundstrokes, Hawk-Eye)
metrics.note: See above.

metrics.definition: Vendor target band for consistent contact height
metrics.note: OnCourtAI goal-setting content ('90-110 cm in 90% of shots'). Vendor figure, not research.

metrics.definition: Contact point distance in front of the body (reference = body/torso plane) for relaxed, balanced pros
metrics.note: Pat Cash argues against reaching far out in front. Reference point is the torso, which explains the small number.

metrics.definition: Contact point distance in front of the lead (front) hip, at about waist height
metrics.note: Coaching guide: '12-18 inches in front of your lead hip, at waist height'. Not measured data.

metrics.definition: Wrist/contact distance in front of the hitting shoulder: vendor scoring bands
metrics.note: OnCourtAI: excellent 20-40 cm, good 10-20 cm, late <10 cm or behind the shoulder line, too early >40 cm (reaching). Same vendor claims Federer/Nadal/Djokovic contact 30-40 cm in front of the body. Product thresholds, unverified.

metrics.note: tenniseye Q&A: ideal is 'slightly in front of the front knee' (also KATO S56); ~40 cm in front of the left knee is described as excessive. Anecdotal.

metrics.note: Review figure; professionals ~33 m/s.

metrics.definition: Racket (head) speed at impact, professionals

metrics.note: Derived: Rybakina 122.6 km/h is 'almost 8 km/h faster than the WTA top-100 average' (AO 2023). Sabalenka 123.4 km/h.

metrics.note: SwingVision ladder (mph): 2.5=41.3, 3.0=43.6, 3.5=44.2, 4.0=45.5, 4.5=47.0, 5.0=48.2. Range = 2.5 to 5.0. Whole-flight average reads ~10% below radar. PlayYourCourt quotes 47-54 mph without method.

metrics.definition: Typical forehand topspin of recreational players
metrics.note: No measured recreational rpm found in this session. Range is from memory of consumer racket-sensor data; low confidence.

metrics.definition: Average groundstroke net clearance (height above the net), men
metrics.note: Hawk-Eye summary. Women 0.77 m. Coaching sites say 2-4 ft (0.6-1.2 m) is a sensible club target and that club players often clear by only ~1 ft (S67).

metrics.definition: Average groundstroke net clearance, women
metrics.note: See above.

metrics.definition: Shoulder alignment angle at completion of backswing (0 = shoulders parallel to net, 90 = side-on, >90 = back partly turned to net)
metrics.note: Reid & Elliott 2002 abstract (high-performance players). One-hander 119.1 deg. Angle convention assumed from the usual 'alignment' definition.

metrics.definition: Shoulder-hip separation angle created in the backswing
metrics.note: Elliott 2006 review: 'one handed ~30 deg; two handed ~20 deg'.

metrics.definition: Time before impact at which horizontal racket acceleration toward the ball begins
metrics.note: Two-handers delay the forward acceleration (0.08 s) compared with one-handers (0.13 s) - a more compact, later swing.

metrics.definition: Additional shoulder rotation used in the acceleration phase compared with a one-handed backhand
metrics.note: Review citing Fanchiang et al. (S32). 2H relies on trunk rotation; 1H on upper-limb segment rotations (S31).

metrics.definition: Non-dominant (top-hand) elbow flexion at impact, eastern top-hand grip (0 = straight)
metrics.note: 16 sub-elite players. Included angle about 119 deg. Top-hand wrist extension 34.7 +/- 16.0 deg.

metrics.definition: Non-dominant (top-hand) elbow flexion at impact, continental top-hand grip
metrics.note: Included angle about 133 deg; wrist extension 43.0 +/- 16.7 deg. Eastern top-hand grip gave faster horizontal racket-head velocity; accuracy and spin did not differ.

metrics.definition: Arm (elbow) included angle at contact, vendor band
metrics.note: OnCourtAI vendor figure. Tennis.com notes some pros have both elbows bent 45 deg or more at contact while Zverev's back arm is straight (S75).

metrics.definition: Torso rotation target for the two-handed backhand
metrics.note: OnCourtAI goal-setting figure; not research.

metrics.definition: Contact point distance in front of the body
metrics.note: Quoted by a coaching site as a biomechanics figure (0.40 m two-handed vs 0.59 m one-handed) without naming the study; an ISBS paper confirms Reid & Elliott 2002 found the one-hander impacts further in front. Coaching consensus: 2H contact is about level with / just ahead of the front hip (S71).

metrics.definition: Average backhand speed, ATP Tour
metrics.note: 66 mph. Sinner and Alcaraz 73 mph (117.5 km/h).

metrics.definition: Average backhand topspin, ATP Tour
metrics.note: 1,977 rpm (Sinner piece) vs 1,775 rpm (Alcaraz piece) - ATP's own articles disagree. Sinner 2,235 rpm; Alcaraz ~2,005 rpm.

metrics.definition: Average backhand speed (all backhand types), NTRP 3.5
Shoulder alignment angle at completion of backswing (>90 = back partly turned to the net)
metrics.note: Reid & Elliott 2002 abstract. Clearly more turn than the two-hander (83.4).

metrics.definition: Shoulder-hip separation angle created in the backswing
metrics.note: Elliott 2006 review.

metrics.definition: Time before impact at which horizontal racket acceleration toward the ball begins
metrics.note: Longer acceleration path than the two-hander - needs earlier preparation.

metrics.definition: Shoulder-line angle to the net at contact (90 = side-on)
metrics.note: Yandell: classic model = shoulders basically perpendicular to the net at contact, opening only a small amount; 'a very common error is turning the hips and shoulders too far too soon so that they face the net at contact'. Feel Tennis says shoulders rotate to ~45 deg even on the one-hander (lower bound).

metrics.definition: Contact point distance in front of the body
metrics.note: See bh2_contact_forward. About 0.32 x height for a 1.83 m player. Korean coaching write-up: about 30 cm in front of the front foot (S53); vendor band 15-25 cm in front (S43).

metrics.definition: Hitting-arm elbow included angle at contact
metrics.note: Vendor figure. Coaching consensus: arm straight before contact; a bent arm at contact is the most common one-hander error (S52). Federer's elbow is bent ~60 deg at the bottom of the swing vs ~20 deg for Gasquet (S65).

metrics.definition: Difference in racket/ball speed and accuracy between one- and two-handed backhands
metrics.note: No significant difference in speed or accuracy (gyroscope study of 20 players; Reid & Elliott report comparable horizontal racket velocities). Choice of backhand is not a power issue.

metrics.definition: Hitting-arm elbow included angle during the forward swing for double-bend forehands (coaching guidance)
metrics.note: Coaching sources disagree: 'bent typically at around 90 degrees for top players' vs a developmental recommendation of 110-140 degrees. Compare with measured 100 (western) to 130 (eastern) at impact (S3).

metrics.definition: Trunk rotation used in the stroke (college players, moderate and maximal power)
metrics.note: 0.51 rad for two-handed vs 0.35 rad (20 deg) for one-handed. Taken from an auto-generated summary of the ISBS paper - NOT verified against the paper's table. Females used ~10% more shoulder rotation; maximal power ~20% more shoulder rotation (same caveat).

metrics.definition: Trunk rotation used in the stroke (college players)
metrics.note: 0.35 rad; see bh2_trunk_rotation_range caveat.

metrics.definition: Average pro groundstroke contact height as a fraction of body height (derived)
metrics.note: Derived: 0.96 m / ~1.88 m (ATP) and 0.94 m / ~1.74 m (WTA). Contact heights from S22; average player heights are from memory. Roughly hip-to-navel level.

metrics.definition: Coaching guideline for forehand contact in front of the lead hip, as a fraction of body height (derived)
metrics.note: Derived from 30-46 cm (S44) for a 1.78 m player. Guideline, not measurement.

metrics.definition: Two-handed backhand contact distance in front of the body as a fraction of body height (derived)
metrics.note: Derived from 0.40 m (S70, secondary) with an assumed 1.83 m player (memory).

metrics.definition: One-handed backhand contact distance in front of the body as a fraction of body height (derived)
metrics.note: Derived from 0.59 m (S70, secondary) with an assumed 1.83 m player (memory). The useful, robust fact is the ordering: one-hander contact is ~0.2 m (about 0.1 x height) further forward than the two-hander.

contact_by_grip.contact_forward: Least far forward - more beside the body, suits a closed stance
contact_by_grip.notes: Lowest isometric force at every contact position in the 100-volunteer test (S36). Face tends to be open, so late contact = high/long ball. Not recommended as a rally forehand grip.

contact_by_grip.contact_forward: In front of the body, around the front hip/knee line
contact_by_grip.contact_height: Knee to waist; best at waist
contact_by_grip.notes: Highest force at early, mid and late contact positions (static test, p<0.001) (S36). More extended elbow (~130 deg) (S3). Good on low and medium balls, harder above the shoulder. Examples: Federer (modified eastern), del Potro.

contact_by_grip.contact_forward: Slightly further in front than eastern
contact_by_grip.notes: Most common tour grip. Beats continental only at the early (forward) contact position in the force test, i.e. it needs contact out in front (S36). Recommended default for recreational players: Tennis Korea clinic says semi-western or eastern for beginners (S86); thicker grips shorten reach.

contact_by_grip.contact_forward: Furthest in front; contact with a more bent elbow
contact_by_grip.notes: Elbow ~100 deg at impact (S3). Hard on low balls (wrist constriction makes flattening out nearly impossible). Thicker grip shortens reach. Example: Swiatek.

contact_by_grip.contact_forward: 5-20 cm in front of the torso (S42); 30-46 cm in front of the lead hip (S44); 20-40 cm in front of the hitting shoulder (vendor, S43); slightly in front of the front knee, 40 cm ahead of the knee is too far (Korean forum, S53/S56)
contact_by_grip.contact_height: Pro average 0.94-0.96 m (S22); works from knee to shoulder (S39)
contact_by_grip.notes: The figures disagree mainly because they use different reference points. No peer-reviewed forehand 'distance in front' value was found. Lateral distance: no numeric source; practical check is elbow not pinned to the torso and arm not fully reaching (S44).

contact_by_grip.grip: dominant hand continental + top hand eastern/semi-western forehand
contact_by_grip.contact_forward: About level with or just in front of the front hip - further back than a one-hander (S71); 0.40 m quoted (S70)
contact_by_grip.contact_height: Waist height is ideal (S46); copes with shoulder-height balls better than the one-hander
contact_by_grip.notes: Top-hand elbow flexion at impact 60.9 +/- 20.3 deg with eastern top-hand grip, 46.8 +/- 20.1 deg with continental (S33). Eastern top hand gives more racket-head speed. Korean sources: top hand semi-western, bottom hand continental; 'left-hand dominant' is the original model (S73).

contact_by_grip.grip: eastern backhand (conservative: Federer, Dimitrov; stronger: Wawrinka; extreme: Gasquet, Kuerten)
contact_by_grip.contact_forward: Clearly further in front than the two-hander: 0.59 m quoted (S70); about 30 cm in front of the front foot (S53); further in front than the forehand (S56)
contact_by_grip.contact_height: Knee to chest; loses leverage above the shoulder (S47, S51)
contact_by_grip.notes: Arm straight before contact (S40, S52). Stronger (more extreme) grips handle high balls better but low balls worse (S77). Shoulders stay roughly side-on at contact (S40).

physics.statement: Upward racket path angle before impact for topspin groundstrokes
physics.note: Elliott & Marsh 1989: 0.48 rad up for topspin, 0.34 rad down for backspin. Reid 2013 review: intermediates ~20 deg, advanced ~30 deg.

physics.statement: Racket face tilt at impact, forward-closed from vertical (topspin forehand)
physics.note: So 'close the face a little' is correct in absolute terms: a good topspin drive has the face 5-15 deg closed while the path rises 20-30 deg. Kwon 2017 (13 collegiate players): only face angle and vertical racket velocity correlated with topspin; no racket variable correlated with accuracy. One summary of Kwon gives 'impact angle 14-33 deg, mean 21' - definition not verified, so not used.

physics.statement: How much the launch angle changes per degree of racket-face tilt vs per degree of swing-path angle
physics.note: Own rigid-impact model (incoming ball 10 m/s, racket 12-30 m/s). Face angle is roughly 3x more influential than path. Tennis coaching sources seen (TennisOne ball-control lesson, ALTA Net News) only say the face is the primary controller and that the racket path dominates more when the racket is much faster than the ball; the popular 75-85% figure is from golf (peer-reviewed golf range 61-83%).

physics.statement: Launch-angle window between 'just clears the net' and 'lands on the baseline' for a ball hit from the baseline at 0.95 m height
physics.note: Own simulation; consistent with Brody: ~8 deg acceptance for a topspin forehand (as cited in S11), window shrinks 43% from 50 to 60 mph (mine: 12.9 -> 7.3 deg), topspin roughly doubles the window at 60 mph and more than triples it at 75 mph vs flat. Recreational pace has a window 2-4x wider than tour pace.

physics.statement: Racket-face error that turns a centred shot into a net or long ball (half the window divided by the face sensitivity)
physics.note: Derived from the two entries above. For recreational players a 5 deg face correction is a meaningful coaching step; for tour pace 1-2 deg matters.

physics.statement: Change in landing depth per 1 degree of launch angle (near the baseline)
physics.note: Cross's notes give ~6 ft per degree of launch angle (context likely a fast shot/serve). At recreational pace one degree is only 0.2-0.5 m.
Geometry: tan(1 deg) x 23.77 m = 0.41 m. Feel Tennis uses a mirror model (1 deg of face = ~2 deg of ball = ~0.8 m). Brody: aiming down the middle gives almost 10 deg either side.

physics.statement: Effect of contact height on the launch window (ball hit from the baseline)
physics.note: A knee-high ball must be launched ~3 deg higher than a waist-high ball just to clear the net; a shoulder-high ball ~3 deg lower. Brody states the same dependence qualitatively.

physics.statement: Effect of hitting position on the launch window (80 km/h, 1,000 rpm, 0.95 m contact)
physics.note: Brody: the further behind the baseline, the bigger the window (waist-high contact). Short balls need more topspin or less pace.

physics.statement: Net clearance and launch angle needed for a given depth at recreational pace (landing distance measured from the hitter's baseline; far service line = 18.29 m, far baseline = 23.77 m)
physics.note: At 70 km/h a ball that clears the net by the tour-average 0.7 m lands ~1.5 m SHORT of the service line; depth at club pace needs 1.5-3 m of clearance (launch 20-27 deg). Do not use the tour net-clearance number (0.69-0.77 m) as a recreational target.

Cross: about 500 rad/s is reachable with ~17 deg forward tilt, especially when the ball is falling and the head rising steeply. Kwon: topspin correlates with face angle and vertical racket velocity, not with horizontal velocity or path direction.

physics.statement: Racket-path difference between long errors and net errors
physics.note: Balls hit long had racket trajectories about 3 deg steeper than balls hit into the net (Blackwell & Knudson; Knudson & Blackwell). Unsuccessful shots also show greater variability in racket-face (orientation) angle; mean face angle differs little between skill levels.

Nine college players: the study found the trade-off only in depth, not laterally, and attributed it to the shrinking geometric window rather than to noisier movement - i.e. hitting harder mainly costs depth control.

physics.statement: Limits of phone pose estimation relevant to this app
physics.note: MediaPipe tennis study (1,281 strokes): switching from metric world landmarks to image-space landmarks dropped cross-player stroke-type accuracy from 83% to 47%. A 2024 validation against Vicon found elbow angles had the largest pose-estimation errors - prefer ratios such as shoulder-to-wrist distance over arm length, and trends over single frames.

physics.statement: Shoulder-to-wrist distance divided by (upper arm + forearm length) as a camera-robust proxy for elbow angle
physics.note: Pure geometry with segment ratio upper arm:forearm = 0.186:0.146 of height (anthropometric ratios from memory). Ratio < ~0.72 at contact suggests a jammed elbow; > ~0.97 a straight-arm hitter.

players.name: Roger Federer
players.style_notes: Usually straight arm, but bends the elbow slightly when jammed; racket face ~11 deg closed at impact; compact, early contact
players.why: Moderate grip and compact preparation are copyable; the straight arm itself needs precise spacing, so copy the turn and the contact in front, not the arm

players.name: Rafael Nadal
players.style_notes: Fully straightened, almost locked elbow; face ~15 deg closed at impact; extreme spin
players.why: Extreme topspin style needs elite racket speed and strength; lasso finish and heavy grip are poor defaults for club players

players.name: Carlos Alcaraz
players.style_notes: Fully extended arm at contact (Mouratoglou); 78 mph and 3,208 rpm average in 2024
players.why: Explosive, very fast swing with straight arm; timing demands are high

players.name: Novak Djokovic
players.style_notes: Benchmark of control and repeatability; full turn with left arm stretched
players.why: Double-bend structure tolerates imperfect spacing; but the near-western grip is harder on low balls - use a milder grip
players.verified_note: Grip verified; double-bend arm supported by only one coaching source (another forum post says he moved toward a straighter arm).

players.name: Jannik Sinner
players.grip: semi-western (some call it an eastern/semi-western hybrid)
players.style_notes: Elbow tucked toward torso at start of forward swing, slight bend at contact; 78 mph / 3,049 rpm vs tour 73 mph / 2,708 rpm
players.why: Structure is sound (Mouratoglou: 'a little bent, like Sinner, is fine') but the racket speed and lag are not reproducible at club level

players.name: Juan Martin del Potro
players.style_notes: Flat, big forehand with eastern grip; listed among straight-arm hitters
players.why: Eastern grip and flatter path are simple; best on waist-high balls, weaker on very high balls

players.name: Daniil Medvedev
players.style_notes: Shoulder turn usually only ~90 deg because the left elbow stays bent and the arm never fully crosses the body
players.why: Idiosyncratic; shows that elite results are possible with a reduced turn, but not a model
players.verified_note: Only the turn description is verified; grip and arm structure not checked.

players.name: Kei Nishikori
players.style_notes: Tight, compact backswing; sets weight on back foot before uncoiling; handles fast balls early; left arm high for balance
players.why: Short take-back that stays on the hitting side = more time, cleaner contact; good model for average-height players

players.name: Roberto Bautista Agut
players.style_notes: Compact swing: elbow stays bent on the take-back, racket stays on the right side of the body; flat ball
players.why: Lesser-known but very repeatable: moderate grip, short backswing, flat drive - close to what a good club forehand looks like
players.verified_note: From a video description and one article; no slow-motion measurement seen.

players.name: David Ferrer
players.style_notes: Lower-elbow take-back kept well outside the body; great timing
players.why: Compact and efficient for a smaller player; relies on footwork more than arm speed
players.verified_note: Mentioned only in a coach commentary.

players.name: Elena Rybakina
players.style_notes: Compact take-back, racket head stays contained behind her, forward contact point, little head movement; 122.6 km/h and 2,286 rpm (AO 2023)
players.why: Simple, quiet technique with flat-ish ball - pace comes from timing and height, not a complicated swing
players.verified_note: Numbers verified (AO); technique description from one coaching blog and a forum.

players.name: Iga Swiatek
players.style_notes: Most 'ATP-like' compact swing on the WTA with heavy topspin (>3,200 rpm reported; another source says ~2,600)
players.why: True western grip makes low balls and timing difficult for club players; copy the compact backswing, not the grip

players.name: Ashleigh Barty
players.style_notes: Compact 'ATP-style' backswing with racket staying on the hitting side
players.why: Short backswing, more topspin, easier to replicate than the long WTA-style swing

players.name: Justine Henin
players.style_notes: Listed among WTA players with an ATP-style (compact, hitting-side) forehand
players.why: Compact swing on a small frame

players.name: Aryna Sabalenka
players.style_notes: Flat power: 129 km/h average at US Open 2024 (above Alcaraz 127, Sinner 125, Djokovic 122); 2,341 rpm at AO 2023
players.why: Low-margin, maximum-pace hitting with about 1,000 rpm less spin than Swiatek - the opposite of what a club player needs

players.name: Jessica Pegula
players.style_notes: Often described as flat and compact (memory), but a forum thread lists her with the long 'WTA-style' backswing group
players.why: Not recommended as a model until verified on video

players.name: Novak Djokovic
players.grip: dominant hand continental + top hand forehand grip (memory)
players.style_notes: Wrist angle fixed through contact, little scooping; can redirect late; widely treated as the benchmark
players.why: Stable wrists and simple shape; copy the full shoulder turn and the firm top hand
players.verified_note: Technique descriptions verified; grip from memory.

players.name: Andre Agassi
players.style_notes: Early preparation, short backswing, full shoulder turn; front arm bent / rear arm straight pattern (forum on Yandell's four variations)
players.why: Short backswing + early turn is exactly what recreational players lack

players.name: Alexander Zverev
players.style_notes: Contacts with the back (top-hand) arm straight or very close to it
players.why: Clean, extended top arm; a tall-player version of a simple drive

players.name: Jannik Sinner
players.style_notes: Both arms bent ('double-bend') structure; 73 mph and 2,235 rpm vs tour 66 mph / 1,977 rpm
players.why: Standard bent/bent structure is the easiest to copy; ignore the pace

players.name: Daniil Medvedev
players.style_notes: Flatter than most, low net clearance, reduced topspin
players.why: Low-margin flat ball is unsafe for club players

players.name: Simona Halep
players.style_notes: Compact, balanced two-hander with early preparation (from memory)
players.why: Efficient technique for an average-height player

players.name: Chung Hyeon
players.style_notes: Korean player known for a powerful two-handed backhand (Korean write-up title seen; content not read)
players.why: Familiar reference for Korean players
players.verified_note: Only the article title was seen.

players.name: Stan Wawrinka
players.grip: eastern backhand, between Federer's conservative and Gasquet's extreme grip
players.style_notes: Straight arm through and after contact; heavier and steadier ball than Almagro's
players.why: Simplest arm structure (straightens early, stays straight); needs a full turn and some strength

players.name: Roger Federer
players.style_notes: Elbow bent ~60 deg at the bottom of the swing and late to straighten, which adds timing complexity
players.why: Late-straightening elbow is hard to time; conservative grip is good for low balls/slice but weaker on high balls

players.name: Richard Gasquet
players.style_notes: Unusual take-back with open racket face; face closed at contact for heavy topspin; elbow bend only ~20 deg
players.why: Extreme grip and big loop demand excellent timing

players.name: Grigor Dimitrov
players.grip: conservative eastern backhand (same end of the spectrum as Federer)
players.style_notes: Classic shape
players.why: Conservative grip is easy to switch to from a continental slice grip; expect trouble on high balls
players.verified_note: Only the grip placement is verified.

players.name: Justine Henin
players.style_notes: Famous one-handed backhand on a small frame (memory)
players.why: Shows the one-hander works without great height or strength if the turn and timing are right

Slow first step / arriving late

checkpoints.reference: At the full turn the left arm is stretched across the body, parallel to the baseline; this adds 10-20 deg of shoulder turn (S38). Nishikori holds the left arm high for balance (S64).
Wrist stays laid back (extended) at impact on most forehands (S3, S38).
Weight is set on the outside/back foot before uncoiling (S64); weight staying back at contact costs control and sends balls long (S69, S55).
Head stays still through contact (vendor: 'rock-solid head position', S43; Rybakina 'little head movement', S63). No measured tolerance found.

Two accepted finishes: extension outward and upward then an over-the-shoulder wrap, or a full 'windshield wiper' where the face turns over and the racket wraps around the shoulder (S39). A finish that stops low or out to the side signals a too-flat swing or leading with the elbow (S69).

Think of the top hand hitting a left-handed forehand with the bottom hand along for the ride (S50); Korean sources call the left-hand-dominant version the original model, though some modern advice is 'both hands equal' (S73).
Shoulders must rotate further than on a forehand to get the racket back (S50); lack of hip rotation is one of the most common faults (S50, S68).
Contact slightly in front at waist height (S46); Djokovic's wrist angle is fixed through contact (S66).
Guides the racket back during the set-up and then stays back as a counterweight; letting it swing forward opens the body early (S51, S53).
Hitting arm straight before contact; hips and shoulders stay perpendicular to the net or open only a little (S40). Bent arm at contact = short or wide ball (S52).
If the eyes follow the ball the shoulders open too early; keep the head at the contact point (S53).
Many club players never let the racket head drop because the hitting arm is too tense (S65).

skeleton_proxies._note: Engineering suggestions for a MediaPipe-only app. Threshold numbers here and in faults[].skeleton_sign are HEURISTIC starting values (not sourced) unless a source value is quoted; calibrate them on pro and club clips processed by the same pipeline.
skeleton_proxies.landmarks_used: MediaPipe Pose indices (from memory): 0 nose, 11/12 shoulders, 13/14 elbows, 15/16 wrists, 23/24 hips, 25/26 knees, 27/28 ankles. Use world (metric) landmarks, not image landmarks (S79).

proxies.name: contact_forward_norm
proxies.how: (hitting wrist - hitting shoulder) projected on the hitting direction at the contact frame, divided by upper-arm+forearm length; also report wrist vs front-hip
proxies.reference: Forehand: wrist clearly ahead of the shoulder/front hip; vendor band 20-40 cm ahead of shoulder (S43). 2HBH about at/just ahead of front hip (S71). 1HBH further ahead: 0.59 m vs 0.40 m (S70).

proxies.name: arm_extension_ratio
proxies.reference: 0.77 = 100 deg elbow (western), 0.91 = 130 deg (eastern), ~1.0 straight arm; 1HBH at contact should be >= 0.97; < 0.72 = jammed (CALC, S3).

proxies.name: shoulder_turn_deg
proxies.how: yaw of the shoulder line (11->12) relative to the baseline, from 3-D landmarks; side-view fallback: apparent shoulder width / true shoulder width

proxies.name: knee_included_angle_deg
proxies.how: hip-knee-ankle angle of the loading leg at the end of the backswing
proxies.reference: about 113 rear / 129-140 front on a forehand (S72, small sample); straight-leg fault > 160 (heuristic).

proxies.name: trunk_tilt_deg
proxies.how: angle of hip-midpoint -> shoulder-midpoint vector from vertical, signed along the hitting direction
proxies.reference: no sourced value; backward tilt at contact is the 'leaning back' sign (S55).

proxies.name: head_stability_cm
proxies.how: displacement of nose landmark from 0.1 s before to 0.1 s after contact
proxies.reference: no sourced value; Rybakina described as 'little head movement' (S63).

proxies.name: swing_rise_proxy
proxies.how: contact wrist height minus lowest wrist height in the forward swing; wrist path angle over the last 3-4 frames before contact
proxies.reference: racket path rises 20-30 deg in topspin drives (S3, S5, S7); the hand rises less than the racket head, so compare against pro clips rather than absolute degrees.

proxies.name: rotation_speed_deg_s
proxies.how: time derivative of shoulder-line and hip-line yaw near contact (needs >= 60 fps)
proxies.reference: ATP pelvis 295, trunk 453 deg/s at impact vs 168 / 292 for high-performance players (S2).

proxies.name: follow_through_reach
proxies.how: does the hitting wrist cross the body midline and reach the opposite shoulder within ~0.3 s after contact
proxies.reference: over-the-shoulder or wiper finish both acceptable (S39).
